lesson_text: "Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably" — Benedick. Themes: love, wit, unconventionality.
canonical_text: "Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably" — Beatrice (Act 5, Scene 2)
note: The essential quotations list attributes 'Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably' to Benedick. It is in fact spoken by Beatrice in Act 5, Scene 2. This is the opposite speaker — a significant factual error that would cause students memorising quotations to give a wrong attribution in the exam. The same misattribution appears in Edexcel L7 (2b88774e) and Edexcel L5 (9440a3db).

lesson_text: "Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably" — Benedick. Themes: love, wit, unconventionality.
canonical_text: "Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably" — Beatrice (Act 5, Scene 2)
note: Same speaker misattribution as AQA L7: this quotation is said by Beatrice, not Benedick. In the essential quotations list it is listed under Benedick's voice. Students who memorise this attribution will produce an incorrect exam answer. The error recurs across AQA L7, Edexcel L7, and Edexcel L5.

lesson_text: When the evidence of their tricked love letters is produced, he [Benedick] says: "Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably".
canonical_text: "Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably" — Beatrice (Act 5, Scene 2). In Act 5.4, it is Benedick who makes the witty remarks about marriage ('man is a giddy thing'), but this line is Beatrice's, not his.
note: The lesson attributes 'Thou and I are too wise to woo peaceably' to Benedick in the context of the Act 5.4 double wedding scene. In fact the line is spoken by Beatrice in Act 5.2 (the garden scene between her and Benedick, before the wedding). The error attributes the wrong speaker and misplaces the scene. This is the third occurrence of the same misattribution across the Much Ado lessons.

lesson_text: The Friar intervenes with reason and compassion. He observes what no one else will: "Is it not Hero? Who can blot that name / With any just reproach?"
canonical_text: "Is it not Hero? Who can blot that name / With any just reproach?" — Hero herself (Act 4, Scene 1). Claudio's reply: "Marry, that can Hero; / Hero itself can blot out Hero's virtue." The Friar's contribution is the 'thousand blushing apparitions' speech.
note: The lesson attributes 'Is it not Hero? Who can blot that name / With any just reproach?' to Friar Francis. In the play, these lines are spoken by Hero herself — one of the very few things she says during her own shaming. Misattributing Hero's only real self-defence to the Friar significantly misrepresents Hero's agency and the dramatic dynamics of the scene. The Friar's contribution to the scene is the 'thousand blushing apparitions' passage, which is correctly quoted elsewhere in the same lesson.

lesson_text: The phrase "O that I were a man" is repeated three times, each repetition more anguished than the last.
canonical_text: Beatrice's speech in Act 4.1 expresses the frustration of being unable to act as a woman, but the exact phrase 'O that I were a man' does not occur as a formal three-part repetition. The speech contains variants of the sentiment but not a neat tricolon of this exact phrase.
note: The lesson claims 'The phrase "O that I were a man" is repeated three times, each repetition more anguished than the last.' Beatrice's Act 4.1 speech does not contain three verbatim repetitions of this phrase as a structured device. The speech powerfully expresses gender frustration, but the specific framing of a formal triple repetition is not supported by the text. Low severity as the broader reading is defensible as an interpretation of the speech's emotional escalation.

lesson_text: Margaret, Hero's gentlewoman, will be persuaded to appear at Hero's window at night, dressed in Hero's clothes.
canonical_text: The text does not state Margaret wore Hero's clothes. Borachio's plan (Act 2.2) involves calling her 'Hero' while she calls him 'Claudio'. The deception relied on darkness, distance, and verbal misidentification. Borachio's Act 3.3 confession: 'partly by the dark night, which did deceive them.'
note: The lesson states Margaret was 'dressed in Hero's clothes' — no textual evidence supports this claim. Shakespeare's text specifies only that Margaret appeared at the window while Borachio called her 'Hero'; the deception operated through darkness, distance (Claudio and Don Pedro watched from the orchard), and Borachio's naming. 'Dressed as Hero' is a stage tradition that many productions use, but it is not in Shakespeare's dialogue or stage directions. The same error appears in Edexcel L3 (725ae709) and Eduqas L3 (fe332c10).

lesson_title: The Gulling Scenes & Don John's Plot
lesson_text: Margaret, Hero's gentlewoman, will be persuaded to appear at Hero's window at night, dressed in Hero's clothes.
canonical_text: The text does not state Margaret wore Hero's clothes. See AQA L3 note.
note: Same unsupported claim as AQA L3: Margaret described as 'dressed in Hero's clothes.' This phrasing is shared across multiple board variants, indicating a single point of origin in content generation.

lesson_text: Don John stages a scene at Hero's window where his accomplice Borachio woos Margaret (dressed as Hero) while Claudio watches from below.
canonical_text: Two errors: (1) 'dressed as Hero' is not in the text; (2) Claudio and Don Pedro watched from the orchard ('saw afar off in the orchard', Borachio's Act 3.3 confession), not from directly 'below' the window.
note: Two separate factual errors in one sentence. First, 'dressed as Hero' has no textual support. Second, 'while Claudio watches from below' misrepresents the staging — Borachio's own confession says Don Pedro, Claudio, and Don John 'saw afar off in the orchard.' The observers were in the orchard at a distance, not standing beneath the window. 'From below' implies proximity directly under the window, which is misleading about the scene's staging and the nature of the deception.

lesson_text: "If I see any thing tonight why I should not marry her, tomorrow in the congregation, where I should wed, there will I shame her." — Claudio (Act 2, Scene 2)
canonical_text: Claudio says this in Act 3, Scene 2 — not Act 2, Scene 2. Act 2.2 is the private Don John/Borachio planning scene; Claudio is not present. In Act 3.2, Don John confronts Claudio and Don Pedro with the accusation, and Claudio responds with this line.
note: The lesson places Claudio's 'I will shame her' speech in Act 2 Scene 2. This is wrong by a full act. Act 2.2 contains only Don John and Borachio planning the window deception — Claudio does not appear in that scene. Claudio speaks this line in Act 3.2, after Don John shows him 'proof' of Hero's supposed infidelity. Students who learn this scene attribution will produce factually incorrect exam responses about where in the play Claudio's decision to shame Hero is made.

lesson_text: Dogberry's language is characterised by malapropisms. He... declares suspects should be 'condemnified' rather than 'condemned'
canonical_text: 'Condemnified' does not appear in the canonical text of Much Ado About Nothing. Dogberry's documented malapropisms include: 'comprehend' (for 'apprehend'), 'aspicious' (for 'suspicious'), 'comparisons are odorous' (for 'odious'), 'dissembly' (for 'assembly'), 'write me down an ass', and 'the most desertless man to be constable.' 'Condemnified' is not among them.
note: The lesson presents 'condemnified' as a genuine Dogberry malapropism for 'condemned.' This word does not appear in any standard edition of the play. It appears to be a fabricated example — plausible in the style of Dogberry's malapropisms but not from the text. The real malapropisms (aspicious, comparisons are odorous, write me down an ass) are well-known and easily verified. A made-up example in a quotation-memorisation lesson is a direct factual error that could mislead students.

lesson_text: Beatrice calls Benedick 'a disease' and compares him to food she finds unappetising. Benedick retorts that he is 'loved of all ladies, only you excepted.'
canonical_text: Both remarks are genuine (Act 1.1), but they are not an immediate exchange. Beatrice's 'disease' speech is addressed to the Messenger before Benedick arrives on stage; Benedick's 'loved of all ladies' is said in a later part of the same scene when he and Beatrice converse directly.
note: The lesson frames these as a paired retort ('calls him... retorts'), implying a direct exchange. In the text, Beatrice's 'disease' comment is to the Messenger (Benedick not yet on stage) and Benedick's 'loved of all ladies' comes later in direct dialogue. Both quotes are accurately transcribed and correctly attributed; the only issue is the suggestion of a direct back-and-forth that doesn't occur as described. Low severity.

lesson_text: Don John tells Claudio that Don Pedro is wooing Hero for himself: 'the Prince woos for himself.'
canonical_text: Don John does not say 'the Prince woos for himself.' That phrase is Claudio's own conclusion (Act 2.1: ''Tis certain so; the prince wooes for himself'). Don John's actual words are: 'Signior, you are very near my brother in his love: he is enamoured on Hero; I pray you, dissuade him from her.'
note: The lesson puts 'the Prince woos for himself' in quotation marks as if it is Don John's speech. The phrase is actually Claudio's own paranoid conclusion, not Don John's words. Don John tells Claudio his brother is 'enamoured on Hero' and urges him to 'dissuade' him. The phrase Claudio jumps to ('the prince wooes for himself') is his own misreading, which is dramatically significant — Claudio is predisposed to believe the worst. Attributing the phrase to Don John as a direct quote obscures this distinction. Low severity as Don John does deceive Claudio in this scene; the distinction is about who says the specific quoted words.

lesson_text: Leonato hints that Beatrice was once hurt by Benedick ('she hath been ever an hour with the Prince's fool')
canonical_text: Beatrice says in Act 2.1: 'he is the prince's jester: a very dull fool.' The 'prince's jester' line is Beatrice's own insult about Benedick to his face (while masked), not Leonato hinting about past hurt. The word is 'jester', not 'fool'.
note: Two issues: (1) 'Prince's fool' should be 'prince's jester' — the actual word in Act 2.1 is 'jester'; (2) the line is Beatrice's own insult spoken directly to Benedick (masked) at the ball, not Leonato hinting about their past. The lesson's framing (Leonato hinting) may conflate this with another reading of past romantic history between them. Low severity as the word difference is minor and the interpretive point about a past connection is a defensible (if not textually explicit) reading.

lesson_text: The phrase "O that I were a man" is repeated three times, each repetition more anguished than the last.
canonical_text: Beatrice's Act 4.1 speech expresses this frustration but does not contain three verbatim repetitions of this exact phrase as a formal tricolon device.
note: The lesson states Beatrice repeats 'O that I were a man' three times in a formal pattern. The speech is powerful and sustained but does not contain three identical repetitions of this phrase. This overstates the structural precision of the speech. The same claim appears in Edexcel L4 (087400b7), suggesting it originated from a shared generation pass.

lesson_text: Claudio reads an epitaph at her monument: "Done to death by slanderous tongues / Was the Hero that here lies."
canonical_text: "Done to death by slanderous tongues / Was the Hero that here lies" — Claudio (Act 5, Scene 3). Correct.
note: No error. Quote and attribution are correct.

lesson_text: "man is a giddy thing, and this is my conclusion" — Benedick (Act 5, Scene 4). Shows self-awareness.
canonical_text: "man is a giddy thing, and this is my conclusion" — Benedick (Act 5, Scene 4). Correct attribution.
note: No error. Quote, speaker, and scene are correct. The lesson does not claim this is the final line of the play.

lesson_text: When Beatrice shifts to verse during her gulling scene (Act 3, Scene 1: 'Contempt, farewell! and maiden pride, adieu!'), the change is striking.
canonical_text: Beatrice's post-gulling soliloquy (Act 3.1) is in verse: 'What fire is in mine ears? Can this be true? / Stand I condemn'd for pride and scorn so much? / Contempt, farewell! and maiden pride, adieu!' Correct.
note: No error. Quote, attribution, act/scene, and the prose-to-verse observation are all accurate.

lesson_text: "I would my horse had the speed of your tongue" — Benedick
canonical_text: "I would my horse had the speed of your tongue, and so good a continuer" — Benedick (Act 1, Scene 1). Speaker and scene are correct.
note: No error. Quote is correctly attributed to Benedick in Act 1.1.

lesson_text: Hero: 'One Hero died defiled, but I do live, / And surely as I live, I am a maid.'
canonical_text: Hero's Act 5.4 speech includes: 'And when I lived, I was your other wife: / And when you loved, you were my other husband' (unmasking) and 'One Hero died defiled, but I do live, / And surely as I live, I am a maid.' Both are present in the scene.
note: No error. Quote and attribution are correct.

lesson_text: Beatrice is the first person to declare Hero's innocence: 'O, on my soul, my cousin is belied!'
canonical_text: "O, on my soul, my cousin is belied!" — Beatrice (Act 4, Scene 1). Correct.
note: No error. Quote and attribution are correct.
